The collapse in 1982 of Souk Al-Manakh, an unofficial stock market in Kuwait City that was housed in an air-conditioned car park.

After the oil price rises of the 1970s, Kuwaitis had plenty of money and few places to put it. The official exchange was tightly controlled, so traders set up their own market for shares in new Gulf companies, many registered in Bahrain or the Emirates with few real assets. Shares were bought with post-dated cheques: pay later, at a much higher price. Prices soared, and at its peak the market's value was said to rank third in the world, after the United States and Japan.

In August 1982 a cheque bounced and the chain of promises broke. Unpaid post-dated cheques came to about 94 billion dollars, several times Kuwait's yearly income. The government stepped in with a costly rescue, and the banks were weighed down for years. It was one of the strangest bubbles in the history of finance.
sum: The collapse in 1982 of Souk Al-Manakh, an unofficial stock market in Kuwait City that was housed in an air-conditioned car park.
